final_proof:
We prove the assertion from the Dedekind-cut construction of the real numbers. Recall that, in this construction, a real number is a subset \(x\subsetneq\mathbb Q\) satisfying: (i) \(x\ne\varnothing\); (ii) if \(r\in x\) and \(q<r\), then \(q\in x\); and (iii) \(x\) has no greatest element. The order is inclusion: \(x\le y\) if and only if \(x\subseteq y\). Rational numbers are identified with their usual Dedekind cuts. This is the standard construction of the ordered field \(\mathbb R\).

Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R\) be nonempty and bounded above. Choose an upper bound \(b\in\mathbb R\), and define

\[
a:=\bigcup_{x\in S}x\subseteq\mathbb Q.
\]

We first verify that \(a\) is a real number. Since \(S\) is nonempty, choose \(x_0\in S\). The cut \(x_0\) is nonempty and is contained in \(a\), so \(a\ne\varnothing\). Since \(b\) is an upper bound of \(S\), every \(x\in S\) satisfies \(x\subseteq b\); hence \(a\subseteq b\subsetneq\mathbb Q\), so \(a\ne\mathbb Q\). If \(r\in a\) and \(q<r\), then \(r\in x\) for some \(x\in S\); because \(x\) is downward closed, \(q\in x\subseteq a\). Finally, if \(r\in a\), then \(r\in x\) for some \(x\in S\). Since \(x\) has no greatest element, there is \(t\in x\) with \(r<t\); then \(t\in a\). Thus \(a\) has no greatest element. All the cut axioms hold, so \(a\in\mathbb R\).

For every \(x\in S\), the definition of a union gives \(x\subseteq a\), and hence \(x\le a\). Therefore \(a\) is an upper bound of \(S\). Now let \(c\in\mathbb R\) be any upper bound of \(S\). Then \(x\subseteq c\) for every \(x\in S\), so

\[
a=\bigcup_{x\in S}x\subseteq c.
\]

Consequently \(a\le c\). Thus \(a\) is no larger than every upper bound of \(S\), while itself being an upper bound. Therefore \(a=\sup S\), proving that every nonempty subset of \(\mathbb R\) which is bounded above admits a supremum in \(\mathbb R\).
